headline: NHTSA plans first marijuana-focused survey of 10,400 drivers
dek: Federal notices reported on 17 November show NHTSA planning a marijuana driving survey for 2027, and pardon certificate requests down 71% to 153.
key_points: NHTSA plans to survey 10,400 drivers in 2027 and 2028 to test whether its impaired-driving adverts reach people about marijuana as well as alcohol; comments close on 11 January 2027.
The last national evaluation of those campaigns, in 2012, did not ask about marijuana at all.
The Justice Department received 153 applications for marijuana pardon certificates in 2026, against 533 in 2025, a fall of about 71%.
Americans for Safe Access asked Congress to fund a federal medical cannabis office inside HHS in the 2027 budget.
body: Two routine federal paperwork notices filed this week say a good deal about where marijuana now sits in Washington. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration wants to run its first national evaluation of impaired-driving advertising that asks specifically about marijuana, surveying 10,400 drivers. Separately, the Justice Department reports that requests for proof of the marijuana pardons issued in 2022 and 2023 have collapsed.

Both details come from notices summarised by The Marijuana Herald on 17 November. Neither changes the law. But one shows a safety agency preparing for a country where more drivers use cannabis legally, and the other shows how few people have used a federal pardon programme that was once presented as a major step.

NHTSA's plan covers its two national impaired-driving campaigns, Drive Sober or Get Pulled Over and If You Feel Different, You Drive Different. According to the Herald's reading of the notice, the agency's last national evaluation of its impaired-driving adverts was in 2012, by telephone, and did not examine marijuana.

The new study would run online through Ipsos's KnowledgePanel, a research panel of about 60,000 people built to be nationally representative. NHTSA plans four rounds in 2027 and 2028, each with 2,600 completed questionnaires. Rounds one and two bracket the Labor Day campaign; rounds three and four bracket the winter holiday push. Adults who drive and drink at least occasionally are eligible, drivers aged 18 to 34 will be deliberately oversampled, and each survey takes about 20 minutes in English or Spanish. The agency expects to approach about 23,072 people to get the 10,400 completed answers.
The exact marijuana questions are not in the filing, and the study still needs approval from the Office of Management and Budget. Comments are open until 11 January 2027 under docket NHTSA-2025-0027.
> A driving study that adds cannabis is not a new law, but it is where future roadside policy gets its data.
## Why it matters to the industry

Impaired driving is one of the most common arguments used against legalization and against expanding sales, and the data behind it is thin. Unlike alcohol, there is no widely accepted roadside test that shows current impairment from THC. A large federal survey on how drivers see cannabis risk, and whether campaigns change behaviour, will feed into state debates on per-se limits and testing. Operators in legal states have an interest in that data being sound, and the comment period is the place to say so.

The Justice Department notice concerns the certificates that prove a person was pardoned under President Biden's proclamations of 6 October 2022 and 22 December 2023, which covered simple federal and District of Columbia marijuana possession and, in the second round, use and attempted possession. People covered were pardoned whether or not they applied, according to the Herald; the certificate is the only paper proof the department issues.

Applications fell to 153 in 2026 from 533 in 2025, according to the notice as described by the Herald. That is a drop of 380, or about 71%. The department does not say when it stopped counting for 2026, so the two figures may not cover equal periods. It cites a diminishing number of applications since the programme began and plans its workload around about 350 a year.

One detail does not line up. The Herald reports that the notice estimates about 30 minutes for each application. The department's own online form, which we checked, still states a burden of 120 minutes per response under OMB control number 1123-0014, which expires on 31 March 2027. The difference matters only for paperwork, but it suggests the form has not been updated to match the notice.

For employers and licensing boards, the guidance on the form is the useful part: a pardon is not an expungement and does not mean innocence, though it can remove civil disabilities and may help with licences, bonding or jobs. That matters in states where cannabis licence applicants must disclose past drug convictions.

Separately, the patient group Americans for Safe Access has published its requests for the 2027 federal budget. Its own page asks Congress to create an Office of Medical Cannabis and Cannabinoid Control inside the Department of Health and Human Services to coordinate research, product safety and clinical guidance. It also wants standard fields in electronic health records that separate medical cannabis use from non-medical use, including route, dose and frequency, across Medicare and Medicaid records, and studies by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services of costs and possible coverage models. These are requests, not law; appropriators would have to write them into bills or reports.

Watch the NHTSA docket until 11 January 2027 for comments from states and industry groups, and for the agency's eventual question list. Watch whether the Justice Department updates its form to match the new burden estimate. And watch whether any of the Americans for Safe Access requests appear in the 2027 health spending bills or their committee reports.
